sourcePdf.methodText:
Put chicken into a large pot; pour 5 cups water over.

Sprinkle onion, paprika, bay leaves, garlic, salt, and red pepper over.

Bring to boil.

Reduce heat, cover, and cook 2 hours until chicken is tender.

Remove chicken pieces; keep warm.

Strain stock and measure.

For each cup of stock, measure 2 Tbsp. flour; blend flour a little at a time into sour cream, beating with a fork.

If too thick, add a little milk.

Stir sour cream mixture into stock.

Simmer 5 minutes until thickened.

Season with salt and paprika, if needed.

Return chicken pieces to sauce, heat through.
ingredientLines: 1 stewing chicken, cut into serving pieces

No optional slow-cooker method is included; all listed steps are part of the main recipe.

sourcePdf.methodText:
STEP 1: Trim excess fat from roast; reserve trimmings. Any of the roasts considered less tender are suitable for pot roasting (braising). These include those cut from the chuck (arm and blade) and round (rump).

STEP 2: Coat all sides of roast with flour, using about 1 tablespoon in all. Coating with flour gives the meat, and later the gravy, a richer brown color. However, you may brown the meat without flour, if preferred.

STEP 3: Heat reserved trimmings in dutch oven until about 2 tablespoons fat accumulate. Discard trimmings. If preferred, you may use 2 tablespoons cooking oil or shortening instead.

STEP 4: Add roast to hot fat. Slowly brown roast on both sides. Use a metal spatula and tongs to turn roast easily. If roast is more box-shaped (as rump roasts often are), brown it on all sides.

STEP 5: Sprinkle roast with a little salt and pepper. Add 1/2 cup water, pouring it directly onto meat, as illustrated. If preferred, for a change of flavor, use apple juice, pineapple juice, beef broth, wine, or beer instead of water. Additional seasonings also may be used, if preferred. Try adding 1 bay leaf, 1/2 teaspoon dried basil, crushed, or 1/2 teaspoon dried thyme, crushed.

STEP 6: Cover and roast in oven at 325 degrees 1 to 1 1/2 hours. Cooking time depends as much on shape of roast as on weight. A flat or thin roast will cook more quickly than a box-shaped roast. Pot roasting refers to cooking at a low temperature in a covered pan with added liquid. This method — sometimes called braising — helps to tenderize meat by breaking down its tough connective fibers.

STEP 7: Add potatoes, onions, and carrots to roast. Since these need less cooking time, they are added toward end of cooking. If preferred, substitute or add any of these vegetables: Sweet potatoes, rutabagas, turnips, parsnips; or celery. If you want to cook roast without added vegetables, simply continue cooking it.

STEP 8: Cover pan and continue cooking about 45 minutes, or until vegetables and meat are tender. Use fork to check doneness, as illustrated.

TIP: Pot roasts also may be prepared atop range. Simply trim and brown as directed. Add seasonings and liquid. Cover and simmer for suggested time. Add additional water as needed to prevent sticking.

To prepare pot roast in an electric slow crockery cooker, first cut roast to fit in cooker, if necessary. Trim and brown as directed. If adding vegetables, slice and place in bottom of cooker; place meat atop. Add seasonings and liquid; cover and cook on low-heat setting 8 to 10 hours.

Heat reserved trimmings in a Dutch oven until about 2 tablespoons fat accumulate. Discard trimmings. If preferred, you may use 2 tablespoons cooking oil or shortening instead.

Add roast to hot fat. Slowly brown roast on both sides. Use a metal spatula and tongs to turn roast easily.

For crockery cooker, first cut roast to fit in cooker, if necessary. Trim and brown as directed. If adding vegetables, slice and place in bottom of cooker; place meat atop. Add seasonings and liquid; cover and cook on low-heat setting 8 to 10 hours.

After browning, pour water directly onto meat. For change of flavor use other liquids such as beef broth, apple juice, or beer.

Vegetables are added near the end of cooking. Then cover pan and continue cooking until both vegetables and meat are tender.
ingredientLines: 2 tablespoons cooking oil or shortening (if preferred)
liquid (such as beef broth, apple juice, or beer)
sourcePdf.notes: Less tender beef roasts are suitable for pot roasting. Before cooking, trim excess fat from roast as directed.
engineeringReviewNotes: No stovetop cooking time or temperature is specified in the manuscript; 2 hours for initial cooking and 30 minutes for vegetables are planning estimates, not source facts.
Crockery cooker method is an alternative and is not included in the main elapsed time.

Ensure meat reaches a safe internal temperature; the manuscript does not provide a temperature guideline.

Soak gelatin in cold water for 10 minutes, then set over hot water until melted.

Add juice drained from cooked, dried apricots.

Combine 10 cups sliced, pared, cored apples (about 5 medium apples) with 1/4 cup sugar, 1 Tbsp. cinnamon; set aside.

sourcePdf.methodText:
Scald 1 1/2 cups milk, add 1 1/2 cups sugar and a little salt.

Allow to become lukewarm, then add 1 cake yeast.

Allow to stand 5 minutes.

Add 1 1/2 to 2 cups flour.

Beat in large bowl.

Cover with towel and stand where no draft to raise.

Beat 2 eggs, 1/2 cup melted butter, flour.

Knead until dough is dry enough (not too dry).

Cover, let raise again until it comes to top of bowl.

Roll out on floured board, add 1/2 cup chopped nuts, 1/2 cup raisins, 1/2 cup brown sugar and butter dough with pastry brush and sprinkle with cinnamon.

Roll like a Jelly roll.

Cut in 1/2 inch slices.

Place in muffin tins with melted butter, syrup, brown sugar, 1 or 2 nuts in bottom.

Put schnecken in and allow to raise (about 1 hour).

Bake in moderate oven---350 degrees.
engineeringReviewNotes: The manuscript does not state baking time, only a moderate oven at 350 degrees; the 25-minute bake is an editorial planning estimate and should be checked by visual doneness.
The manuscript gives no times for the first raise, second raise, or most mixing/kneading stages; those durations are planning estimates, not source facts.
Manuscript directs adding flour both before the first raise (1 1/2 to 2 cups) and again with eggs and butter; add the second flour gradually because the amount is unspecified.
Manuscript says '1 cake yeast'; no yeast type, proofing method, or temperature is given, so follow package guidance for the yeast used.
Manuscript places 1 or 2 nuts in the bottom of each muffin tin in addition to filling nuts; this is represented as written.
Do not add optional slow-cooker or other alternative methods; none are present in the source and none are scheduled.
